1.text:
Is Space Really Empty?

Deck 17 followed stars from birth to death. Now we look at the space between them. It's tempting to think of it as pure nothing, a black emptiness between the bright dots. But it holds a surprising amount of stuff.

In this deck we'll explore interstellar gas, the gas and dust that stars are born from and return to. We'll visit the heliosphere, the giant bubble our Sun blows around itself. We'll ride along with Voyager, the spacecraft now crossing into interstellar space. And we'll meet visitors that came to us from other stars. The big question: is space really empty?

2.text:
Is Space Empty? True or False

Let's start with a quick hook. Mark each statement T for true or F for false.

The space between stars is a perfect vacuum. There is dust floating between the stars. Our Sun sits inside a giant bubble it made. A human-made probe has reached interstellar space. Objects from other stars have flown through our Solar System.

Write down your answers and don't change them. We'll check every answer by the end of class.

3.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Write these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can describe how thin the interstellar medium is. I can compare the phases of interstellar gas. I can explain how dust dims and reddens starlight. I can explain how the 21-cm line maps hydrogen. I can describe the Local Bubble and our local cloud. I can label the layers of the heliosphere.

I can trace the Voyagers' crossings into interstellar space. I can explain what "one light-day away" means. I can compare the three known interstellar objects. I can use eccentricity to tell bound from unbound orbits. I can judge the 'Oumuamua alien-probe claim. And I can build a scale model from the Sun to Proxima. These connect to Indiana standards ES.1.1, ES.1.3, ES.1.5 and ES.2.2.

4.text:
Almost Nothing, but Not Nothing

How empty is empty? Typical interstellar gas has about 1 atom per cubic centimeter. That's a space about the size of a sugar cube holding a single atom. Compare that to the air you breathe, which packs about 1019 molecules into every cubic centimeter. That's ten billion billion!

So interstellar space is far emptier than any vacuum we can make on Earth. But the galaxy is so huge that this thin stuff adds up. The interstellar medium (ISM) is about 99% gas and 1% dust, by mass. It's mostly hydrogen and helium, just like the stars.

Spread over the whole galaxy, it adds up to about 15% of the mass of the stars. And it's recycled. New stars form from it, and dying stars return gas and dust to it, as you saw in Deck 17.

5.text:
Part 1: The Stuff Between the Stars

Here's a puzzle. How do you photograph something that doesn't glow?

Most interstellar gas is invisible to our eyes. In Part 1 we'll explore the gas and dust between the stars and learn how astronomers see what's dark. The trick, as always, is using different kinds of light and different telescopes.

6.text:
Four Kinds of Interstellar Gas

Interstellar gas is mostly hydrogen, but the same hydrogen can be at very different temperatures. Astronomers sort it into four phases.

Molecular clouds are about 10 K. They're cold, dense clouds of H₂ and dust where stars are born, and we see them by radio light from CO molecules. Neutral hydrogen is 100 to 8,000 K. It's single H atoms spread through the disk of the galaxy, and we see it with the 21-cm radio line.

Ionized hydrogen (H II) is about 10,000 K. It's gas lit up by hot young stars, and it glows red in visible light. Hot gas is about 1 million K. It fills bubbles heated by supernovae, and we see it in X-rays.

Did you know? K stands for kelvin, and 0 K is absolute zero, the coldest anything can possibly be.

7.text:
What Dust Does to Starlight

Dust may be only 1% of the interstellar medium, but it changes how we see the sky in three ways.

The first is extinction. Dust blocks light, so dark clouds look like holes in the Milky Way. The second is reddening. Dust scatters blue light more than red, so stars behind it look redder. It's the same reason sunsets are red: our air scatters blue light out of the beam.

The third is an infrared glow. Dust is warmed by starlight and glows in infrared, and infrared telescopes can see through it. That's how Webb's infrared images, from Deck 16, show stars inside dusty clouds that look dark in visible light.

Did you know? The famous Horsehead Nebula is a dark dust cloud seen in silhouette against glowing gas behind it.

8.text:
The 21-cm Line

The 21-cm line is radio waves at 1420 MHz from cold hydrogen atoms. It was predicted by van de Hulst in 1944 and first detected by Ewen and Purcell in 1951.

This is why it's so useful. Radio passes through dust, so we can map hydrogen across the whole galaxy, not just the part near us. These maps traced the Milky Way's spiral arms.

There's a bonus. Doppler shifts in the line show how the gas moves. That will let us measure how fast the galaxy spins, the rotation curve you'll see in Deck 18.

Did you know? Any single hydrogen atom gives off a 21-cm photon only about once every 10 million years. But there are so many atoms that the signal is strong.

9.text:
Our Neighborhood

The Sun sits inside the Local Bubble, a region of hot, thin gas about 1,000 light-years across. A string of supernovae hollowed it out over about the last 14 million years.

As its edge expanded, it pushed gas together. Young nearby stars formed on its surface, like foam collecting on the edge of a bubble.

Right now the Sun is passing through a smaller cloud inside the bubble, called the Local Interstellar Cloud, at about 7,500 K.

Did you know? Scientists have found radioactive iron-60 in deep-sea crust on Earth, left from nearby supernovae a few million years ago.

10.text:
Check for Understanding

Let's see if the ideas stuck. Why can radio astronomers map hydrogen across the whole galaxy when visible-light telescopes can't?

Is it A) radio waves pass through dust, B) hydrogen only glows in radio, C) radio telescopes are bigger, or D) dust is hot? Look back at Slides 7 and 8 and choose the best reason.

11.text:
Part 2: The Sun's Bubble

Where does the Solar System end? It sounds like a simple question, but the answer depends on what you measure.

In Part 2 we'll explore the heliosphere, the bubble the Sun blows with its wind, and follow the two spacecraft that left it.

12.text:
Layers of the Heliosphere

Starting from the Sun and moving outward, the heliosphere has five zones. 1, the solar wind: charged particles stream out at about 400 km/s. 2, the termination shock: the wind suddenly slows, at about 85 to 95 AU. 3, the heliosheath: slowed, hot, tangled wind.

4, the heliopause: where the solar wind meets interstellar gas, at about 120 AU. 5, interstellar space: the denser, colder gas of the local cloud. Remember, one AU is the Earth-Sun distance, 150 million km.

Think of water from a faucet hitting a sink. It spreads in a fast thin stream, then suddenly slows at a ring, then reaches the edge. The heliosphere shields the planets from many galactic cosmic rays. Its exact shape, a comet-like tail or something rounder, is still debated. Your turn: why is the heliopause not the end of the Solar System?

13.text:
Voyager Crosses the Line

In 1977, Voyager 1 and 2 launched. Decades later, they reached the edge of the heliosphere.

In December 2004, Voyager 1 crossed the termination shock at 94 AU. In August 2007, Voyager 2 crossed the termination shock at 84 AU. On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause at 121.6 AU, the first human-made object in interstellar space. On November 5, 2018, Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause at 119 AU.

How did scientists know Voyager 1 had crossed? The plasma around it became about 40 times denser. Solar particles dropped and cosmic rays from the galaxy jumped up.

Did you know? Scientists measured that density from a "ringing" in the plasma around Voyager 1, set off by a burst from the Sun.

14.text:
One Light-Day Away

Around November 18, 2026, a radio signal will take 24 h to travel one way to Voyager 1. At that point Voyager 1 is about 25.9 billion km from Earth. That's one light-day, how far light goes in a day.

Think about what that means. If mission control sends a question, the answer takes two full days to go there and back.

Voyager is getting old. Its power supply weakens every year, so NASA turns off instruments to save energy. But it's still sending data from interstellar space.

Did you know? The nearest star is about 1,550 light-days away, so Voyager has traveled less than 0.1% of the way there.

15.text:
Check for Understanding

Time to check your heliosphere map. What marks the heliopause?

Is it A) where the solar wind meets interstellar gas, B) where the Sun's gravity stops, C) the orbit of Neptune, or D) where the solar wind first slows down? Look back at Slide 12 and choose carefully. One wrong answer describes a different layer.

16.text:
Part 3: Visitors from Other Stars

Here's a mystery. Say a rock zooms through the Solar System. How can you tell it isn't from here?

In Part 3 we'll meet three objects that came from somewhere else. They're samples of other star systems that delivered themselves, free of charge.

17.text:
The Three Known Interstellar Objects

So far, we know of three interstellar objects. Their names start with "I" for interstellar.

1I/'Oumuamua was found on October 19, 2017, by Pan-STARRS in Hawaii. It's long, tumbling, and had no visible tail. Its eccentricity was about 1.2. 2I/Borisov was found on August 30, 2019, by Gennady Borisov, an amateur astronomer. It's a comet with a tail, and its eccentricity was about 3.4.

3I/ATLAS was found on July 1, 2025, by the ATLAS survey in Chile. It's an active comet, with an eccentricity of about 6.1.

Did you know? 'Oumuamua is Hawaiian for "a messenger from afar arriving first."

18.text:
Eccentricity Tells the Story

Eccentricity (e) is a number that tells how stretched an orbit is. It's the key to spotting a visitor.

When e = 0, the orbit is a circle. Between 0 and 1, it's an ellipse, so the object is bound to the Sun and keeps coming back. When e is above 1, the path is a hyperbola. The object passes through once and leaves forever.

All three visitors had e above 1 and arrived too fast to belong to our Sun. Compare that to planets, which have e close to 0. A value of 6, like 3I/ATLAS, means the path is barely bent by the Sun at all.

19.text:
Was 'Oumuamua an Alien Probe?

'Oumuamua did something strange. It sped up slightly as it left. Why?

The alien idea came in 2018. The push had no visible gas or dust tail, which comets usually have. One paper said it could be a thin light sail, a spacecraft pushed by sunlight. The idea was widely reported in the news.

Then scientists dug in. The push is real, confirmed by 2018 measurements. But in 2023, scientists showed that ice could release hydrogen gas that is hard to see. That explains the push with no aliens. A bold idea was published, then tested, and a natural explanation fits the data. That's good science working the way it should.

20.text:
Scale Model: Sun to Proxima

Let's feel these distances. Use a scale of 1 cm = 10 AU. Place a dot for the Sun and start measuring.

Neptune at 30 AU is 3 cm away. The heliopause at about 120 AU is 12 cm. Voyager 1 at one light-day is about 173 AU. And Proxima Centauri, the nearest star, is about 268,000 AU, which is about 268 m away.

Record A, your scale distances, and B, what surprised you. Where would Voyager 1 land, and how far would you have to walk to reach Proxima?

21.text:
Exit Ticket

You've traveled from the Sun's wind out into interstellar space. Show what you learned with five questions.

1, about how many atoms are in a cubic centimeter of interstellar gas? 2, why do stars behind dust look redder? 3, name the layers of the heliosphere, from the Sun outward. 4, how did scientists know Voyager 1 had entered interstellar space? 5, why do astronomers think 'Oumuamua came from another star?

Then go back to your true-or-false answers from Slide 2. How many did you get right?

22.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.1: explain how we study space by observing every kind of light, using different telescopes and tools. ES.1.3: show how energy cooled into protons and early elements, how those formed huge stars and galaxies, and how gravity pulls clouds of gas together into stars and galaxies. ES.1.5: show how stars, planetary systems, multiple-star systems, star clusters, galaxies and galaxy groups fit inside one another, and how big each one is.

ES.2.2: describe the kinds of objects in the solar system, like planets, moons, comets, asteroids and protoplanets. Know that planets have been found orbiting other stars, and even drifting with no star at all. Describe how our solar system is organized, including terrestrial and Jovian planets, asteroid belts and the Oort Cloud.
